## Nature is a key part of our cities

![Qi of the City by Nicole Yu & Betty Woo](presentation_imgs/tnoc-p16.jpg){fig-align="center"}

::: notes
-   the integration of nature with the built environment creates novel
    ecosystems
-   requires inter and trans disciplinary studies to be understood
:::



## There are many benefits of urban nature, which are disproportionately provided by trees {.smaller}

![The Nature Conservancy](presentation_imgs/city.webp)

::: notes
-   ecosystem services - regulating & cultural
-   vary across spatial and temporal contexts
:::

## My goals

:::: incremental 
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}


1.  Integrate temporal heterogeneity and historical conditions

2.  Use interdisciplinary approaches and perspectives 

3.  Assess benefits of understudied types of green infrastructure 

4.  Contribute a multi-scale, cross-city study to the Canadian urban ecology literature
:::
::::

## We asked:

:::: incremental
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}
1.  What are the effects of historical land-use on current park forest
    structure, diversity, and consequently the capacity to provide
    cooling?
2.  How do surrounding communities differ around parks of each
    historical land-use type, and what are the implications for
    equitable access to cooling?
:::
::::

## Put parks everywhere! ... with intentional, community led approaches

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Historical data provides useful ecological context

-   Parks have the capacity to provide cooling, regardless of historical
    land-use

-   To improve environmental equity, green space development must be
    community led and paired with stronger housing regulations
:::

## Interview results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
-   19 ecosystem services mentioned 
-   Many of which are cultural 
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: table-s3

library(scales)
library(dplyr)
library(flextable)

interviews <- read.csv('presentation_imgs/es_coding.csv') %>% 
  select(-c(TotalPeopleMentions))

t <- col_bin("Greens", domain = 0:75)

interviews %>% 
  arrange(desc(TotalMentions)) %>% 
  flextable() %>% 
  bg(
    j = c("TotalMentions"),
    bg = t, part = "body"
  ) %>% 
  set_header_labels(
    EcosystemService = "Ecosystem service",
    TotalMentions = "Total number of mentions"
  ) %>%
  set_table_properties(
    opts_html = list(
      scroll = list(
      height = "500px",
      freeze_first_column = TRUE))
  ) %>% 
  fontsize(size = 18, part = 'all')



```
:::

##  {background-image="presentation_imgs/dogwood.png"}

:::::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
::::: columns
:::: {.column width="90%"}
::: {style="background-color: #c0c0beff; opacity: 80%"}
-   Green alleys are providing important benefits 

-   Different management approaches result in different benefits 

    -   Montréal is more variable and also more flexible
    -   TR is less variable but less able to adapt to resident needs

-   Right now, green alleys are providing more biodiversity support than ecosystem services  with respect to **benefits provided by trees**

-   We recommend a bottom-up approach paired with **expert support** and **ongoing funding** to maximize the potential of green alleys
:::
::::
:::::
::::::

## We asked 


:::: incremental 
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}
1.  What is the relative contribution of street trees to predicting urban heat and air pollution at different scales when compared to urban form and sociodemographics? 

2.  What are the relationships between important predictors of temperature and air pollution in different cities and across scales? 
:::
::::


## We measured temperature, air pollution, ecological form, urban form, and sociodemographics across 7 Canadian cities {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}

![](presentation_imgs/seven-cities.png){width="80%"}

::: 

::: {.column width="40%"}

::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}

- Ecosystem service indicator: land surface temperature,  air pollution (CO, NO2, SO2, UV, O3)

- Ecological form: street tree diversity/size/density, greenness  

- Urban form: building cover/height, road size/density, greyness 

- Sociodemographics: income, race/ethnicity, immigration status, housing 

:::

:::

:::::


## We measured our variables at multiple scales {.smaller}

::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}

## Predictive models can help us identify areas for further research  

::::: incremental

:::: columns

::: {.column}

- We need to assess scale-specific interventions for temperature and air-pollution related issues in cities 

- Trees are most likely affecting the environmental conditions much more than is indicated in this study 

- More multi-scale, multi-service studies are needed in Canada


::: 

::: {.column}

![](presentation_imgs/cherry-blossom.jpg){fig-align="right" width="50%"}

::: 



::::


:::::


## Thesis Conclusions {background-image="presentation_imgs/milkweed-2_sarahodriscoll_photography.jpg"}

- Historical conditions influence the present day 

- Understudied, small forms of green infrastructure have the potential to provide many benefits but need management and research attention 

- Spatial scale is an important consideration when intervening in Canadian cities
